judgments.forked_readings_summary:
No material fork — all four read the task identically: run the preflight /preflight:migrate skill end-to-end on the legacy "account" (AccountLookup) .NET service through the full pipeline (config/service resolution → unique-per-attempt branch cut → Phase 1 discovery via discovery-analyst + spec-analyst with the immutable legacy baseline, DB name-contract, and read-only SQL extraction scripts → single human go/no-go gate → Phase 2 generation-spec-driven .NET 10 execution incl. verbatim DB identifiers, WIRE-B golden, CI workflow + vendored parity scripts → post-Phase-2 dependency refresh and parity verification → 7-check pre-handoff gate → handoff to fix-and-close → one clean PR against the canonical repo). This matches the actual SKILL.md flow.

Differences are emphasis/granularity, not scope:
1. Pre-requisites HALT framing: interpretation #3 leads with "this code-forge repo has no mode=migration config / legacyRepoPath, so the realistic first action is to HALT at the Pre-requisites gate." Interpretations #1, #2, #4 carry the exact same fact but in their assumptions block ("this is a consumer-side invocation; code-forge itself has no migration config"), treating it as context rather than the headline action. Same understanding, different foregrounding — not a different task.
2. Surface-naming granularity: #2 and #3 enumerate framework-internal file paths (lib/parity-check.sh, examples/rubrics/rubric-migration-dotnet.md, skills/migrate/SKILL.md); #1 and #4 frame surfaces by code-layer (controller, data-access, intermediary-decoupling, container/IaC). #1 and #4 also explicitly name the downstream-intermediary decoupling surface (which is genuinely in Phase 1 step 3). Both cover the same surface set at different altitudes.

All four converge on every load-bearing behavior: never skip Phase 1; never self-run a sub-agent (dispatch failure = COMPLETION-BUG that STOPS the run); generation spec PASTED verbatim or STOP; byte-for-byte DB identifier fidelity; immutable legacy baseline committed alone first; parity exit-2 is terminal and the agent NEVER writes parity-clean (only parity-override-requested); coverage floor met by adding tests only; reachability traced before flagging a phantom gap; commit is NOT completion (the SessionToken failure mode); PR opened with explicit --repo canonical; one service per PR; humans merge, agent never force-pushes or touches the read-only legacy repo. The shared assumptions also align: account→AccountLookup, target .NET 10, SQL Server legacy, unattended-except-Phase-1-gate.

No material fork — all four read the same task: run /preflight:migrate end-to-end on the legacy "account"/AccountLookup .NET service (Phase 1 discovery via discovery-analyst + spec-analyst, Phase 2 generation-spec-driven .NET 10 execution, parity verification, 7-check pre-handoff gate, handoff to fix-and-close to land one clean PR). Surfaces and core behaviors are in full agreement and match SKILL.md faithfully: Phase 1 never skipped; sub-agent dispatch failure is a STOP-worthy COMPLETION-BUG never self-run; generation spec mandatory + PASTE-verbatim-or-STOP; byte-for-byte DB identifier fidelity; legacy baseline committed alone and immutable; reachability annotation kills phantom gaps; coverage floor via added tests only; parity exit 2 is terminal with parity-override-requested (never parity-clean); commit is not completion (must open PR with --repo canonical, never merge/force-push). The only divergence is emphasis: interpretation #3 (with a lighter touch from #4) foregrounds that code-forge itself has no mode=migration config and would HALT at the Pre-requisites gate, while #1/#2 treat the run as occurring inside a properly configured consumer repo. But all four independently flag the same config prerequisite and all four explicitly assume a migration-configured consumer is the intended context — so #3's HALT framing is a more cautious surfacing of a shared assumption, not a different task. A second minor variation: #1 and #4 add a "comparison surfaces" lens (controller, data-access, downstream-decoupling) that #2/#3 fold into the same name-contract/wire/parity items — same surfaces, different grouping.

All four read the SAME task: run the preflight /preflight:migrate skill end-to-end on the legacy "Account"/"AccountLookup" .NET service — Phase 1 discovery (discovery-analyst + spec-analyst sub-agents in isolated context, dependency-map.json, readiness score, immutable legacy behavior-spec.json committed alone, legacy-db-name-contract.md with REACHABLE/NOT-REACHABLE annotations, targeted read-only SQL extraction scripts) → single Phase 1 human gate → Phase 2 verbatim-paste from the dotnet-service generation spec (.NET 10) with core migration/modernization/tests-to-coverage-floor/WIRE-B golden/IaC/container/per-service CI workflow + vendored parity scripts → post-Phase-2 dependency-map refresh + behavior-spec-current.json + parity-check.sh → 7-check pre-handoff gate → handoff to /preflight:fix-and-close (Stage 1 → push → Stage 2 Copilot loop) opening a single PR against the canonical repo via --repo. Surfaces match (orchestrator, two analyst sub-agents, generation spec, parity engine, DB name-contract/extraction, WIRE-B serialization, CI workflow, fix-and-close handoff, checkpoint). Key behaviors match across all four: never skip Phase 1, never self-run a sub-agent (dispatch failure = COMPLETION-BUG that STOPS), generation spec mandatory and PASTE-verbatim (STOP if none resolves), verbatim DB identifier fidelity, immutable legacy baseline, parity exit-2 is terminal and agent never mints parity-clean (only parity-override-requested), coverage floor via ADDING TESTS ONLY, reachability-trace before flagging a phantom gap, commit-without-push is not done, --repo guard against legacy origin, never force-push/merge, one service per PR. The ONLY divergence is emphasis, not task: interpretation 3 (and to a lesser degree 1, 2, 4 in their assumptions) flags that THIS repo (code-forge, the framework source) has no mode=migration config, so a literal run here would HALT at the Pre-requisites gate; interpretation 3 makes that HALT a first-class in-scope behavior, while 1/2/4 treat it as an assumption that the request is a consumer-side invocation where config exists and proceed to describe the full pipeline. This is a minor behavioral variation in framing the entry condition, not a different task — all four still describe the same end-to-end pipeline.
